title: The scheme and its gates
paras: Let's start with the scheme and its gates. The permitted development order grants planning permission nationally for building work within the curtilage of a house, across nine classes — extensions and alterations, extra storeys, roof enlargements like dormers, other roof alterations, porches, outbuildings, hard surfaces, chimneys and flues, and antennae. I'll keep the citations out — the class letters and statutory references live in the written guide.

Three gates before you open any class. One: houses only — flats, maisonettes and a house divided into flats get nothing. Two: if the dwelling only exists because of a change-of-use right — a barn under Class Q, an office under Class MA — it's shut out of householder rights entirely; no extensions, no outbuildings, not even a porch. Three: the use has to genuinely be as a house. The rights attach to the use, not the bricks.

Every main allowance is measured against the original house — as first built, or as it stood in 1948 if it's older. Anything added since counts against your allowance today, whoever built it, permission or not — a previous owner's seventies rear addition can leave you no Class A headroom at all, and the deeds won't say so.

Designated land — conservation areas, National Parks, the Broads, National Landscapes, World Heritage Sites — runs tighter throughout: under Class A it strips cladding, side extensions and multi-storey rear extensions, and the dormer class is gone entirely. Rights can also be pulled on any land by an article 4 direction or a condition on a permission. So the sequence: confirm it's a house and how it became one, pin down the original house and its land, check nothing's removed the rights, find what's already built — then measure.

title: Class A: extensions day to day
paras: Now Class A, the everyday extensions — enlarging, improving or altering the house. A single-storey rear extension goes four metres beyond the original rear wall on a detached house, three metres on anything else, up to four metres high. Within two metres of a boundary, the eaves can't exceed three metres.

More than one storey and it tightens: no more than three metres beyond the original rear wall, at least seven metres from the rear boundary, roof pitch matching the house as far as practicable. Upper floors trigger the neighbour conditions — any side-elevation window obscure-glazed and fixed shut, unless the opening parts sit above one point seven metres from the floor.

Side extensions are single storey only, four metres max, no wider than half the original house. On designated land there's no side extension, no multi-storey rear extension, and no cladding — stone, artificial stone, pebble dash, render, timber, plastic or tiles.

Over all of it sit the general limits: nothing forward of the principal elevation where it fronts a highway, nothing higher than the existing roof, eaves no higher than the existing eaves, building coverage in the curtilage capped at fifty per cent excluding the original house, and no verandas, balconies or raised platforms — raised meaning over thirty centimetres. Materials to match, conservatories aside. Measurement decides these: heights off the highest adjacent natural ground, depth from the original rear wall, not the current one. A wraparound must meet side and rear limits at once, which it rarely can. Over by any margin and the whole extension is unauthorised — no minor breach here.

title: The larger home extension route
paras: The larger home extension route doubles that single-storey rear allowance — eight metres detached, six on anything else — through the neighbour consultation scheme. The right only exists if you follow the process to the letter, it's off on designated land, and it's single-storey rear only.

You submit a written description of the depth beyond the original rear wall, the maximum height and the eaves height, with a site plan and the adjoining addresses. The authority notifies the adjoining owners and occupiers, who get twenty-one days to object. If any adjoining neighbour objects, the authority assesses the effect on adjoining amenity — and only that — then grants or refuses.

Work can begin on one of three events only: written notice that approval isn't required, written notice granting it, or forty-two days from receipt with no decision. Silence after forty-two days is a lawful start — unusual among prior approval regimes. Build in accordance with the details submitted or approved; the stated dimensions are the enforceable envelope. And the assessment, where triggered, is confined to adjoining amenity — design, character and highway objections get no purchase.

title: Roofs: Classes B and C
paras: On to the roof. Class B is the roof enlargement — dormers and hip-to-gable conversions — within a cubic allowance: forty cubic metres on a terrace, fifty on anything else, measured externally. It's cumulative, so any previous roof enlargement, by any owner at any time, eats into it. And it's off on designated land entirely.

The enlargement can't exceed the highest part of the existing roof, or extend beyond the plane of the roof slope on the principal elevation where it fronts a highway. Other than hip-to-gable work, set it back at least twenty centimetres from the original eaves, measured along the slope. Materials to match, side windows obscure-glazed and fixed shut, no veranda, balcony or raised platform.

Class C is the alteration that doesn't enlarge — rooflights, mostly: no more than fifteen centimetres beyond the roof slope, and not above the highest part of the roof. Class C survives on designated land, which is why rooflights stay feasible in conservation areas when dormers don't. Where the ambition is a whole extra floor, the choice is Class B's cubic arithmetic, self-assessed, against the additional-storey route, which goes through prior approval with the authority judging external appearance. Run both calculations first.

title: Class AA: additional storeys
paras: That additional-storey route is Class AA, brought in in 2020: up to two extra storeys on a house of two or more, or one on a single-storey house — but the gates rule out a lot of the stock. The house must have been built between 1948 and October 2018, can't exceed eighteen metres total height once extended, and it's off on designated land and off for houses created by the change-of-use rights.

Unlike the rest of the householder rights, nothing happens without prior approval, assessed on a long statutory list — external appearance, impact on neighbours' amenity, air traffic and defence where relevant. So the authority effectively holds a design judgment over appearance, and refusals are routine.

Two things people miss: there's a condition to notify the authority on completion — unique among these rights, easily forgotten. And the class points at national policy by the Framework's publication date, so those references get refreshed as new Frameworks come out — read it against the current position. There's also no government technical guidance on Class AA; the old householder guidance predates it and was never revised, so your only sources are the order itself and the appeal decisions.

title: Outbuildings and surfaces: E and F
paras: Now outbuildings and surfaces. Class E covers buildings, enclosures, pools and containers for a purpose incidental to enjoying the house — garden office, gym, workshop, pool. Incidental is load-bearing: primary living accommodation isn't incidental, so an outbuilding that's really a bedroom, or a self-contained annexe, falls outside whatever the drawings call it.

The limits: single storey only; four metres max with a dual-pitched roof, three otherwise, two and a half metres for any part within two metres of a boundary; eaves capped at two and a half metres; nothing forward of the principal elevation; and the same fifty per cent curtilage coverage cap it shares with extensions, so the old shed and the new garden room count together. On designated land, and in National Parks, the Broads and National Landscapes, siting and size tighten further. Raised platforms over thirty centimetres are out here too, which catches decking, and an outbuilding can't house an antenna. And the incidental use persists: a building put up lawfully as a store becomes unlawful the moment it turns into a dwelling, enforceable as a material change of use.

Class F is hard surfaces for the enjoyment of the house, with one operative condition, at the front: a new or replacement surface between the principal elevation and a highway bigger than five square metres has to be porous, or drain to a permeable area within the curtilage. It's there for surface-water flooding — and tellingly, enforced most often after the flood.

title: Porches, chimneys, antennae — and proving it
paras: Finally the small classes, and proving it. Class D is the porch outside any external door — three square metres of ground area at most, measured externally, three metres high at most, no part within two metres of a boundary with a highway. Class G covers chimneys, flues and soil pipes, provided they don't rise a metre or more above the highest part of the roof, with siting restrictions on designated land. And Class H allows up to two microwave antennae within size limits — broadly a metre, only one over sixty centimetres — a thirty-five litre capacity cap, chimney-mounting rules, and visibility restrictions on designated land, plus conditions to site them out of sight and remove them once they're no longer needed.

And it's all self-assessed: no one checks it, nobody issues anything, and owner confidence isn't a legal status. The only thing that certifies lawfulness is a lawful development certificate — one for proposed works, one for works already done — decided on the balance of probabilities, against evidence.

That discipline matters at sale, where purchasers' solicitors increasingly want proof that unconsented works were lawful. Where a dimension sits near a limit, the certificate before you build is the cheap insurance; the one after a dispute is the expensive kind. And the edge of the subject: these rights answer the planning question, nothing else. Building regulations, the Party Wall Act, private covenants, drainage easements, protected species law all apply on their own terms, and none of them has read the permitted development order.
